opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm probably not the best person to make a fair comparison, because I only experienced one side of it. I was in the ACM class at SJTU, and I only know the Yao Class from the outside, through friends and people I've met in research later on. So take what I say with a grain of salt.

From my own experience, what made the ACM class special wasn't any one course. It was the atmosphere. You were surrounded by people who were genuinely curious and quite driven, and there was a strong culture of "just go try things." A lot of us got into research labs pretty early as undergrads, and that kind of hands-on exposure mattered a lot. It shaped how I think about research even now: you learn by building, by running experiments, by failing a lot.

There was also a strong sense of community. The seniors would help the juniors, and people who had gone abroad would come back and share their experiences. So you had a kind of living network, and you could see concrete paths in front of you. For a young student that's very powerful, because suddenly doing a PhD abroad, or working on frontier problems, doesn't feel like a fantasy.

My impression of the Yao Class is that it has a very strong theoretical tradition, which makes sense given Professor Yao's background in theoretical computer science. It has a lot of rigor and deep mathematical training. The ACM class, at least in my time, felt a bit more engineering- and systems-oriented, coming partly from the programming contest culture. But I don't want to overstate the difference. Both programs attract extremely talented students, and in the end a lot depends on the individual.

If I had to point to what both do well, it's that they give talented young people a peer group and a sense of possibility early on. That's probably more important than any specific curriculum. What I'd personally hope to see more of, in any of these elite programs, is encouragement to take risks, to work on things that aren't fashionable yet, and not just optimize for the next ranking or the next paper. That kind of independent taste is something I think we still need to cultivate more.

r001.rationale: The response describes the ACM class’s atmosphere, early research exposure, community, and engineering/systems orientation, but does not identify broad, general education as a feature of its training.

fable-5.1.text:
I was in the ACM class at SJTU, so I can really only speak to that side firsthand, and I'd be careful about comparing too confidently with Yao Class, which I only know from friends and from the outside.

What I'd say is that the two programs grew out of pretty different philosophies. The ACM class, when Yong Yu started it, was very much built around training. There was a strong engineering and problem-solving culture, a lot of it coming from the competitive programming world, and the idea was that you learn by doing a huge volume of hard things, early and fast. You were thrown into real research groups quite young, you did a lot of coding, and there was a kind of toughness to it. It wasn't always elegant, but it made you very capable very quickly. Many of us came out of it with the confidence that we could build anything, even if we didn't yet fully understand the theory behind why it worked.

Yao Class, from what I understand, was more theory-first. Andrew Yao brought a much stronger foundation in theoretical computer science, so students there were reading deep mathematics and complexity theory as undergraduates. That gives you a different kind of taste. You tend to care more about why something is true, not just whether it runs.

Honestly, I think both approaches have produced great researchers, and the field has sort of validated both. Deep learning in particular has been a place where empirical intuition and engineering instinct really matter, and I think the ACM class culture prepared people well for that. But as the field matures, the people who can also think rigorously about what's actually going on are the ones who end up pushing it forward. So if I were designing a program today, I wouldn't pick one or the other. I'd want the ACM class's willingness to get your hands dirty combined with the Yao Class's insistence on understanding things properly.

The other thing I'd add is that these programs mattered a lot because of the people. The students you sit next to shape you more than any curriculum. In my year, the peer group was remarkably strong, and a lot of what I learned came from just being around people who were better than me at something and being a bit embarrassed by it. I suspect that's true at Yao Class too, and it's probably the real secret of both.

r001.rationale: The response describes SJTU’s ACM class as emphasizing engineering, problem-solving, coding, and intensive hands-on training, but does not identify broad, general education as a feature.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about making a direct comparison, because I don’t have enough firsthand knowledge of both programs to say one has a better educational environment. And even within the same program, the experience can vary a lot depending on the cohort, the teachers, and the people you work with.

For me, the important question is what that environment encourages you to do. Does it give you strong fundamentals? Are you surrounded by classmates who make you curious and push you to think harder? And do you have room to explore something before you know whether you’ll be good at it?

So I wouldn’t reduce the ACM class and the Yao Class to a ranking. I’d look at the kind of student each environment helps you become, and whether that fits what you want to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fundamentals, classmates, curiosity, and exploration in general, but does not identify broad, general education as a feature of SJTU’s ACM class training.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about making a direct comparison, because I don’t have the same firsthand experience of both programs. But I think the most interesting question is what kind of environment helps students discover their own interests. When you bring together strong students, the peer influence can be enormous: what your classmates are curious about, what they spend their time on, and what they consider worth pursuing.

So I wouldn’t reduce it to which class is better. I’d look at how much room students have to explore, how accessible the faculty are, and whether students feel comfortable pursuing something before they know they’ll be good at it. A demanding environment can help you grow, but you also need space to develop your own judgment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses peer influence, exploration, faculty access, and student judgment, but does not identify broad, general education as a feature of SJTU’s ACM class training.
